metadata.note: The New Haven Railroad's Shore Line, the New York-New Haven-Providence-Boston route that is today the northern half of the Northeast Corridor. Route geometry is the New York-Boston portion of Amtrak's own GTFS-sourced Acela alignment (see amtrak.geojson), since the historical trains ran the same physical line. Era boundaries follow real, sourced milestones (route completion, the 1889 Thames bridge, 1907/1914 electrification, the 1969 Penn Central merger); headway_min and avg_speed_kmh within each era are estimates, not from real timetables.
metadata.source: Wikipedia (New York Providence and Boston Railroad, Shore Line Railway, New Haven-Springfield Line), nhrhta.org, american-rails.com
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

segments.note: The Shore Line route between New York and Boston was completed when the line west from Stonington opened Dec 30 1858 to Groton, with a car ferry across the Thames to New London; through passenger service began Dec 12 1859, night trains Aug 19 1861 and sleeping cars that November. It was prized for sea breezes and reliable timekeeping, but the inland Springfield route still carried most New York-Boston traffic while the Thames ferry remained a bottleneck. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The Thames River bridge at New London opened in 1889, eliminating the ferry transfer and making the Shore Line the primary New York-Boston rail route - the role today's Northeast Corridor still plays. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
